title: Genetics and genomic medicine in Slovakia
abstract: Provision of medical genetics services in the Slovak Republic has a well established organisational structure, network of providers, personnel and methodical conditions which ensure high-level services. The main limiting factor is finance allocated to these services by insurance companies; far below eligible demand. The Slovak Republic (SR) is a small sovereign state in Central Europe which gained independence on the 1 January 1993 by separation from the Czech/Slovak Federal Republic. From 2002, the SR was divided into eight semi-autonomous Regions (“krajov”); each named after its principal city; with their self-governing bodies referred to as Upper-Tier Territorial Units (VÚC). These regions are subdivided„ into a total of 79 districts (“okresov”). The Slovak Republic joined the European Union on 1st January 2004 and was included in the Eurozone on 1 January 2009. SR land area covers 49,036 square kilometers with a 2011 population of 5,397,036 (www.portal.statistics.sk) in three main ethnic groups: 80.7% Slovaks, 8.5% Hungarians, and 2% Romany. The Roma percentage is actually greater than this; estimated between 7.5% and 8.8%, as many Roma declared their census ethnicity Slovak or Hungarian dependent on their habitat, and a further 380,000 appear not to have furnished 2011 census particulars. Romany presence on Slovak soil was first recorded in 1322 AD, and significant migration waves were later reported in the 16–17th centuries from Western Europe, and again in the second half of 19th century from Vlachia and Moldavia after slavery's abolition. Romany people currently inhabit ~300 SR settlements. While Slovak and Hungarian families prevailingly have two children, and rarely three or more, Roma families have a significantly higher number; often ten or more. The right of all SR citizens to health care is constitutionally guaranteed; with general health services regulated by the following main 2004 laws: (1) Law 577/2004 regulates the extent of healthcare financed from public health insurance, and (2) Law 578/2004 defines the public network of healthcare providers, the licensing conditions for founding healthcare facilities. Personnel qualification requirements and continued education, and a quality control system overseeing healthcare duties of both provider personnel and professional associations. These laws have been updated several times; with healthcare service management delegated to the Ministry of Health (MH) and the Bureau for Supervision of Healthcare Provision, and the institution of healthcare facilities founded by both state and private corporations. SR healthcare service expenses are financed from public health insurance based on agreement between healthcare providers and insurance companies. There are currently three SR insurance companies: one state founded and two private companies. All employed Slovak inhabitants are obliged to pay a legally assigned health insurance fee from their income, freely choosing their contracted insurance company; while the state pays for children, students, and pensioner groups. Healthcare services financed by individual insurance companies are substantially similar, with exceptional services negotiated with providers for patient payment, and those unavailable in the SR can be accessed internationally with insurance company negotiation and consent. Although the Slovak republic has no specialized healthcare laws regulating the provision of genetic services over and above the quoted 577/2014 and 278/214 laws, generalized rules are implemented under Health Ministry powers and guidelines The most important of these is titled “The Conceptual Framework of Medical Genetics.” This was originally issued in 1972; with its most recent amendment in 2013 defining the following: (1) the content and extent of medical genetics services, (2) the criteria for building the insurance provider network, (3) approved healthcare facility types with infrastructure and personnel requirements for their creation and function, and (4) a quality control system ensuring ongoing personnel education. A further regulation level in genetics services provision is overseen by the Chief Specialist for Medical Genetics appointed by the Ministry of Health. The main duties include regulating interaction between healthcare service providers and the MH, cooperating with MH issued regulations which demand a high professional level of genetic services provision and supervising regulation adherence. Artificial pregnancy termination in SR is regulated by law no. 73/1986, which allows interruption without providing a reason until the 12th gestational week, while serious fetal pathology or endangering the mother's life allows pregnancy termination until the 24th gestational week. Maternal informed consent is required for all terminations. Medical genetics legislation empowered in 1964 demands compulsory reporting of congenital abnormalities Here, data collection and evaluation are performed by the National Health Information Centre (NHIC, www.nczisk.sk). This mandated reporting of genetic disorders was instituted in 2014 and the Slovak Republic Genetic Registry created. NHIC also conducts the following registries; the National Registry for Congenital Heart Defects (established in 1992), the National Cancer Registry – including rare cancers – (established in 1976), and the National Child Diabetes Mellitus and Neonatal Diabetes Registry (established in 1986). Current European Union (EU) healthcare provisions demand complex management of patients with rare diseases. In compliance, the SR Government passed its 2012 resolution entitled “National strategy for improvement of healthcare provided to patients affected with rare disorders for years 2012–2013;” whereby Health ministry experts instituted the “National plan for improvement of healthcare provided to patients affected with rare disorders in SR.” It is estimated that ~80% of rare disorders are genetic in origin. Slovak facilities providing medical genetics services employ the following graduate professionals; (1) physicians specializing in clinical medical genetics and (2) nonmedical university graduates in genetics, biochemistry, microbiology, and molecular biology. Medical genetics has been an acknowledged medical speciality in Slovakia since 1972. The undergraduate curriculum in all medical faculties includes general genetics; with medical genetics clinical applications broached in individual clinical branches. The main medical genetic specialist education is conducted at the postgraduate level over 4 years and is completed by passing board examinations and defending a written dissertation. NHIC 2012 data indicate 39 physician specialists in medical genetics in 23 facilities; which approximates 1one specialist for 138,000 inhabitants. In contrast, nonphysician professional postgraduate education lasts 3 years and postgraduates achieve specialization in “analytical methods in medical genetics” by passing board examinations and defence of a written dissertation. Although these medical genetics specialists outnumber physicians, no precise data are available. In addition to graduate professionals, personnel with secondary school education, nurses, and laboratory technicians are employed at facilities providing medical genetics services. These employees access education systems to achieve speciality in their respective genetic services fields. The Slovak Society of Medical Genetics (SSMG) is a professional association for all medical genetics personnel and for professionals in alternate medical fields interested in medical genetics. SSMG has a common history with the Czech Society of Medical Genetics. It began here in 1967, and although the Czech and Slovak medical genetic societies separated in conjunction with 1993 statehood, they maintain close collaboration. Current SSMG membership varies from 110 to 120; with the main purpose of promoting member's professional skills and their activity in organized workshops, seminars, and congresses. The initial congress was organized in 1974, and this annual event was then renamed “The Izakovič's Memorial” in 1990 to honor Professor Viliam Izakovič; founder and outstanding expert in Slovak medical genetics. This annual memorial congress encompasses all fields of medical genetics and it currently alternates between SR cities, with an average 100 oral and poster presentations. Specialized diagnostic centers, especially in university and faculty hospitals, have been created for frequently occurring genetic disorders. These supply complex management for patients from wide regional and national areas; with three centers for cystic fibrosis, two for phenylketonuria, and one each for hemophilia, alkaptonuria, muscular dystrophies, neurofibromatosis, and rare metabolic disorders. In addition, patients with monogenic forms of cancers are treated in SR oncologic clinics, where karyotyping, FISH and molecular genetics testing are available. Medical genetic service providers are either state-owned or private companies which meet law no. 578/2004 criteria and conform to the Conceptual Framework of Medical Genetics. These services are financed from public health insurance by agreement between provider and insurance company; with patients bearing the cost of unreferred and unlegislated care. While in SR genetic testing is also offered by domestic and foreign companies via “direct-to-consumer” testing, no precise data on its prevalence are available. The availability of publicly funded diagnostic genetic testing follows a similar distribution pattern to that for general public medical services. Cytogenetic traditional karyotyping and FISH testing is widely available for both clinical and prenatal diagnosis. Molecular karyotyping (qPCR) is mostly available only in private laboratories, where chromosomal microarray analysis is offered by two laboratories with different platforms, and cytogenetics for oncology and onco-hematology is performed in specialized oncology clinic laboratories. Initial diagnostic DNA molecular testing in SR was performed in 1987 for prenatal diagnosis of cystic fibrosis by linkage to DNA polymorphisms. The scale of genetic disorders and molecular techniques have significantly expanded, so that current diagnostic testing is amenable for more than 300 monogenic disorders; covering all frequent disorders and a relatively large number of rare ones. While limited insurance-approved and patient-funded testing is available for Slovak patients internationally. In SR diagnostic molecular testing for alkaptonuria is so well established because of its high incidence that worldwide samples are tested in our laboratories. A broad scale of progressive molecular genetics techniques are employed, including: PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction), MLPA (Multiple Ligation-dependent Probe Amplification) and fragment analysis modifications, Sanger's sequencing, expression analysis, micro deletion/duplication and CNV microarrays; with massive parallel sequencing (NGS) also available to a limited extent. These tests are mostly offered by private providers, because running these facilities is very expensive and the majority of state-funded healthcare providers are deeply in debt. Hence, finance-shortage constitutes the main limiting for molecular genetic testing factor in SR. Insurance company budgets assigned to genetic testing are well below the medically justified demand, ensuring that waiting-time for some tests ranges from several months to a year. Prenatal diagnosis has been widely available in Slovakia since initial karyotyping in the mid 1970s. Prenatal testing must be indicated by a medical genetic specialist based on established and unacceptable fetal risk, family history, molecular testing, or biochemical and ultrasonography screening. Genetic counseling is mandatory, both before and after prenatal testing; with all incurred expenses covered by public health insurance. Samples obtained from amniocentesis or CVS (Chorionic Villus Sampling) are typically used in karotyping chromosomal analysis. Rapid interphase fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) screening for chromosomal aneuploidy, evaluation for specific microdeletions or microduplications, microarray and other innovative molecular techniques are also available. Although some private fertility clinics offer preimplantation genetic testing, they send their samples abroad because test costs are not covered by SR public health insurance. Neonatal screening policy in SR (NBS) was officially established by the Ministry of Health in 1985. Its latest modification was in 2012, increasing the number of screened disorders to the 14 listed in Table 1 (Statute 42, Bulletin of MH SR, parts 39–60). Screening in Slovakia is provided by the National Newborn Screening Centre (NNSC) in Banská Bystrica; coordinated with three Regional Recall Centres; and NNSC is a functioning member of EUNENBS (European Union Network of Experts on Newborn Screening). In addition to the listed diseases, every newborn is screened for hearing impairment and hip dysplasia; with over 90% further screened immediately after birth by ultrasonography for somatic CNS (Central Nervous System) malformations, cardiovascular system anomalies, and obstructive uropathy. These latter screenings, however, do not form part of official governmental policy. Gynecologists are obliged to offer every pregnant woman biochemical and ultrasonograpic screening for developmental anomalies; but acceptance is voluntary. The most frequently used approach is combined first trimester screening for pregnancy-associated plasma protein-A (PAPP-A); and free beta human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) or total hCG with or without nuchal translucency (NT). Integrated screening with or without NT for total human chorionic gonadotropin, maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein and unconjugated oestriol is also conducted. The increasing quality of biochemical and ultrasonographic screening is well documented by statistics. While 1991 prenatal karyotyping from biochemical and ultrasonographic analyses based on estimated increased risk comprised ~30% of all prenatal tests, this increased to 61% in 2013. Similarly, the 2002 average of 2.1% identified prenatal chromosomal aberrations increased to 5.1% in 2013. Prenatal testing acceptance ranges from 80% to 90% in SR large towns, and 50–60% in rural regions. This difference is attributed to possible greater religious ideology and relatively less biology and genetics knowledge in rural communities. Pregnant Slovak woman over 35 years are legally compelled to undergo prenatal screening, regardless of anticipated outcomes. The SR non-Romany population exhibits a similar scale and incidence in the majority of genetic disorder as other European populations. The most prevalent monogenic disorders include cystic fibrosis, phenylketonuria, hemophilia A and B, spinal muscular atrophies, Huntington's chorea, Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy, myotonic dystrophy, monogenic hearing loss, neurofibromatosis type 1, FRAXA, Wilson's disease, Charcot-Marie-Tooth syndrome, etc. In contrast, SR alkaptonuria prevalence is an exception, with the second highest world incidence of 1 in 19,000 inhabitants. This compares unfavorably with the worldwide average of ~1 in 250,000: and hence specialized alkaptonuria research and health care has been paramount. Slovak researchers have played a significant role in elucidating alkaptonuria genetics and instituting treatment (Zaťková et al. 2000a,b). Here, the Piešťany spa, under the auspices of the National Institute for Rheumatic Disorders, is well renowned for its specialized health-team alleviating affected patients’ rheumatic symptoms. The Slovak Romany form a typical small genetically isolated population, with almost 100% endogamy, a high inbreeding ratio and all characteristics encountered in such populations. It has vast monogenic disorder frequency compared to its non-Romany counterparts. Examples include: (1) Romany suffer one of the highest phenylketonuria incidences in the world; at 1 in 1000 newborn; ten times the frequency registered in the majority SR population. This is caused by founder mutation R252W (Feráková et al. 1992); (2) primary congenital glaucoma is present in 1 in 1200 of their newborn; caused by founder mutation E387K in the CYP1B1 gene (Plášilová et al. 1998, 1999); (3) monogenic hearing impairments are very frequent; with mutations in GJB2 and MARVELD2 genes identified in affected patients. While founder mutation IVS4+2T-C is identified in the MARVELD2 gene (Šoltýsová et al. 2012), the scale of mutations in the GJB2 gene is broader with mutation W24X dominating (Minárik et al. 2003); and (4) the recently identified retinitis pigmentosa type caused by founder mutation c. 316C>T in the RDH12 gene is noted (Ficek et al. 2003). In direct contrast, cystic fibrosis, one of the most frequent monogenic diseases in European populations, is currently undetected in the Romany population. The National Health Information Centre (NHIC) holds most national health registries. Its National Registry for Congenital Disorders established in 2011 from the former Register of Congenital Anomalies in Newborns (1964), highlights the significant proportion of congenital anomalies of genetic origin (www.nczisk.sk). This records that 1953 of the total 55,585 SK newborns in 2012 had diagnosed congenital anomalies. Table 2 hereunder lists the distribution of these congenital anomalies by type and specification. The parents of these children are referred to local outpatient clinics for medical genetics services and family planning advice. Medical genetics research in SR is primarily conducted in state institutions; with private company participation almost negligible. Most research is concentrated in Slovak Academy of Sciences entities which include, amongst others: (1) The Institute of Molecular Physiology and Genetics focuses on monogenic disorders; (2) The Institute of Experimental Endocrinology focused on metabolic disorders; and (3) The Institute of Experimental Oncology researches monogenic oncologic disorders. Significant research covering practically all fields of medical genetics is promoted in medical universities and university hospitals. Progressive technological equipment from EU Structural Fund projects is well established, including state-of-the-art massive parallel sequencing devices. The main factor limiting research effectiveness is insufficient finance allocated by research agencies to run this equipment. The two state grant agencies in SR are VEGA (a joint research agency of the Ministry of Education and Slovak Academy of Sciences for institution from these two resorts), and RAPRD (Research Agency for Promoting Research and Development). These agencies cover grants to all SR institutions; both state and private. Provision of medical genetics services in the Slovak Republic has a well-established organizational structure, network of providers, personnel and methodical conditions which ensure high-level services. The main limiting factor is finance allocated to these services by insurance companies; far below eligible demand. Consequently, test waiting-time ranges from several months to a year, with similar protracted introduction of the latest technology and tests in diagnostic practice. These latter are mostly developed and offered by private providers; often via “direct-to-consumer” testing, because state providers are deeply in debt. Medical genetics intervenes in all current and future fields of medicine and its impact can only increase exponentially. Therefore, if the Slovak Republic wishes to emulate well-developed states, our insurance companies must re-evaluate their medical genetics services finance policies. None declared.

title: The Crucible
abstract: The following symposium was conducted by Lenke Wood's AP English class at Moses Brown School in Providence, Rhode Island, after attending a performance on 2 October 2019.[Editor's Note: Given the frequency with which Miller's The Crucible is taught in high school classrooms, it was a delightful experience to receive this selection of responses to a live production of the play (as opposed to the students just reading the text) by this evidently insightful group of teens. While the accessibility and immediacy of Eric Tucker's engaging production clearly made an impression on all, it is interesting how far their thoughts spin out from what they witnessed. Many felt almost a part of the production, drawn in and able to make clear connections to the present day; several even reevaluate their own responsibility to get engaged in a way that would have made Miller proud. Collectively they consider every aspect of the performance—staging, acting, lighting, sound, costume—and offer a series of fascinating ideas regarding how the play reflects on a variety of topics, including sexism, religion, and notions of self-suppression. We see here ample evidence of why Miller's nearly seventy-year-old play remains both relevant and worthy to be taught as well as performed. My thanks go to their lucky teacher, Lenke Wood, who rounded up these wonderful responses for the Journal.] —Susan C. W. Abbotson Performance Review EditorBedlam's production of The Crucible incorporated its audience into the play in a number of powerful ways. Sitting in my chair in the second row, I could have sworn I was on stage with the cast throughout the entirety of the play. The play began with the cast members shaking hands, as if to welcome the audience into their group. I was greeted with a warm, firm handshake and a friendly smile from Tituba. Soon after, characters emerged from the seats around me. There was no curtain raised or division between the actors and audience. The stage wasn't high up; we were all on the same level. The physical nature of our unity turned emotional as the play advanced. I felt encircled by the production: lights were shone into the audience, the cast ran up and down the stairs, noises came from behind, next to, and in front of me. It was a surreal feeling. I felt like a bystander to the mistreatments happening on stage. Every cast member was an accomplice to the hangings, and so was I. A feeling of responsibility for the injustices happening on stage extended to me through the direction of this production, mirroring the liability of the people of Salem. We were all responsible now. —Lucy HowlandIn Bedlam's production the audience was welcomed by cast members literally shaking our hands. This formality immediately made us just as much a part of the play as the characters were, and thus introduced the predicament of our role in witnessing the injustice during the Salem witch trials. As an audience, we are expected to sit and watch a play, but perhaps Eric Tucker intentionally involved us in his production to expose the challenge of speaking up when you know something is wrong. Characters' actions reinforce this challenge. Throughout The Crucible, the protagonist, John Proctor, disrespects women. In a scene where Proctor and Mary are arguing, the rest of the cast is on the stage as well: an odd but meaningful choice. When Proctor winds up to strike Mary, the cast's response is subtle, and unexpected. Instinctively, each character shields their eyes, or looks away, and the audience obviously does not challenge the script, but Bedlam's production challenges us to reevaluate our own confidence, moral responsibility, and decision making in society. —Amanda StecklerStudents' whispers and giggles quieted as the cast of Bedlam's The Crucible made their way in and around the audience, looking us in the eyes when they shook our hands, providing a very brief and unexpected moment of intimacy between spectator and spectacle. After a few moments, the actors dispersed, and the lights dimmed. The play was about to begin. It opened with a tableau; then the first scene unfolded with all of the cast remaining on stage throughout. Proctor arrived. Abigail flung herself to the floor. The cast scattered about the set, faces pressed into the walls. Each detail seemed so very calculated, all the way down to the lighting. When the action picked up so did my heart rate. Accusations were flung around the room. Everyone was excited. The chilly air became warmed by the heat of squirming bodies and gut-wrenching yells. As the production unfolded, the contained tableau seemed to spill out into the audience. It felt as if the entire space was simultaneously unfathomably large and claustrophobically small. The intimacy made it feel like you were implicated in the plot of the play but unable to do anything to intervene. The early established closeness with the actors, even when they withdrew to the stage area, made the experience even more cathartic. When Mary Warren was called to the stand and forced to prove she could faint on command, she looked around the audience with fearful eyes, groping for comfort. The actress looked me directly in the eyes, and I will never forget how the intensity in her gaze made me feel so helpless. Bedlam's production highlights how an audience member can be simultaneously involved and yet passive in their immobility. The production itself and its intensity made for highly involved audience participation. At times, it felt absolutely personal. However, the fact that the audience by social convention cannot intervene made its members feel more like implicated bystanders rather than separated spectators. —Jessica KellyWhen in the audience of Bedlam's production of The Crucible, one was not simply an idle observer. The second an audience member entered the theater, they were greeted with a handshake from one of the characters; personally, I was greeted by Mr. Parris, who also sat next to me during the court scenes. Because of this, the audience instantly built a connection to the characters within the production. This became incredibly valuable as the play continued, and we were forced to reckon with the troubling decisions made by the characters. As the production continued, the audience was drawn closer and closer to the characters, both literally and emotionally. In a literal sense, after a short intermission, the seats on the floor were rearranged to be closer to the action and diagonally facing the stage; this made the audience feel as if they were crowding the production. This also further strengthened the physical (and therefore emotional) connection between the characters and the audience. This connection reached its greatest height during the court scenes, when the audience was very close to the tribunal, and lights were often pointed straight at the audience. Because the audience felt like they were part of the production when the lights were shone on them in this way, they were forced to think about why they were not acting up and saying anything about the atrocities being committed. By very explicitly drawing a connection between the audience and the play, Bedlam asks its audience to think about who had the power to stop the witch hunts in Salem and why everyone chose to be passive bystanders instead of taking a stand. —Kolya Markov-RissAt the beginning of Bedlam's production of The Crucible, the stage was inset in the wall, appearing to the audience like an individual room within a doll house. Everything was neat, organized, and contained within this small, cramped space, and all of the actors were also squished into this petite, recessed area. Everyone seemed to be going about their business, moving robotically, repeating movements over and over just like a drinking bird toy. One actor began soaking a rag in water and wringing it out repeatedly, another tossed an apple up into the air before catching it again many times over. I felt that this design represented Salem before the trials begin: calm and robotic, nobody daring to step out of place. As the play progressed, the actors escaped the confines of the room, spilling themselves and the props out onto the floor right next to where the audience was sitting. By the end of the play, everything from within the original set was strewn across the floor—chairs, tables, papers, and the actors themselves. The characters entwined with the audience, sitting in chairs uncomfortably close to us as if to say, “This is about you too.” An incredibly effective and discomforting technique. —Carson SwiftClose your eyes and imagine this. Piercing screams echo against the neighboring walls. All the stage lights in a room blare in the faces of the actors. The rubber flat shoes of women stomp against wooden tables as the balls of men's feet clash against the cold stage floor. Absolute chaos. It was nearly impossible to distinguish voices from each other. Out of the madness though came the shrill voice of Caroline Grogan, the incredible actress portraying Mary Warren. As she succumbed to Abigail Williams's immense power, she admitted, “I love God, I bless God. Abby, Abby, I'll never hurt you more!” She had had enough of John Proctor's misogynistic chokehold. We see this powerful character, whose independence had become hushed by John Proctor's abusiveness, begin to diminish as she falls into the hands of this society's misogyny. All of the women stood on the wooden tables, ironically becoming tall above the men. Everyone but John Proctor and Governor Danforth viewed these women from the floor, staring up in complete awe and anguish. This beautiful scene, with its various levels, emphasized how the women, with this new power, had become the ones “running the show” in Salem. Though it was saddening to witness Mary Warren's false confession, it was simultaneously cathartic to see her standing above John Proctor as she saved herself from imminent death. —Melissa EaBedlam's production applied light nontraditionally. The plays I have seen typically use stage lights from above to illuminate a room or character. However, the cast themselves used several handheld light fixtures to highlight their castmates. While there were some stage lights for the general lighting of the room or scene, certain cast members picked up handheld lights to hold under the faces of their castmates. This added a more dramatic effect because of the harsher direct lighting. It made characters appear more immersed in their monologues. Sometimes, members would situate the light toward the front of the stage closer to the audience, but face it in the direction so that the light would shine on themselves. This light shone in the same direction from which we, the audience, watched the production, which indicated that the light shining onto the actors symbolized what we were watching and thus projected us as bystanders to the play. Another nontraditional aspect of the play was that as scenes changed, there was no dimming of the lights to give actors or the crew time to rearrange the furniture. The cast changed the scene accordingly as they were acting, which created a more fluid transition from scene to scene. Many times, they used the ruckus of moving the furniture across stage or stacking it to add to the commotion of either an argument or the court scene. In the broader sense, this loudness spoke to the hectic times of the witch trials. Everyone was yelling at each other, and no one was safe or at peace in the few moments of quiet. —Ashley QiuA distinctive aspect of Bedlam's production was the manner in which the set shifted to reflect the developing chaos of the play over time as well as the deeper truths brought to light by this retrogression. The unraveling of order that occurred within the small Puritan town of Salem took multiple shapes, but the way the whole of the cast ended up traveling barefoot or in socks by the conclusion of the second act was perhaps the most striking. At first, this choice appeared simply to mirror the greater disarray visible throughout the set, and while it certainly served to do so, it also spoke to something more intricate and vulnerable about the characters as a whole. Their bare feet united them in a primal, intimate way, and in a play in which divergence and polarization are central, this was consequential. There was a sense of primitive reversal and sameness that was not nearly as visible within the text. With their feet planted on the ground, each cast member touched the same surface, and in the rising havoc, the powerful were dethroned and the oppressed were elevated. It was a both humanizing and sobering take on the conclusion of the play. —Abigail GerrishOne of the most fascinating elements of Bedlam's production of The Crucible was their representation of how religion, and the lack thereof, was perceived by the townspeople of Salem. In the beginning of the production, John and Abigail engaged in a conversation about their relationship. Bedlam's choice to display the rest of the cast in a cluster at the back, united by song and prayer, dealt with the perception and reality of religion within the town. As the couple discussed their forbidden, adulterous relationship, the huddled cast physically hid their eyes and ears from the conversation, singing louder as the exchange became more uncomfortable. This physical representation of hiding from an uncomfortable situation is representative of the way that people throughout the town created perceptions of themselves that portrayed them as perfect, practicing Christians, while in reality there was more going on behind the scenes that did not support such a vision. Although the whole witch hunt was supposedly rooted in religion, in the ways it was pursued, the true essence of a compassionate and loving Christianity was completely lost. This particular scene nicely illustrated how townsfolk can blind themselves to sins happening under their very noses, singing hymns to bind themselves together in their willful ignorance and present a front of insincere religiosity. Their determination to do this also showed how they embraced the posture of practicing Christians to create a cult mind-set that would restrict them from having to think for themselves and so allow “the church” and its officials to do their thinking for them. —Caroline WorrellOne striking part of Bedlam's production of The Crucible was its incorporation of music. One distinctive scene in which music was used was when the teenagers began accusing others of witchcraft at the end of act 1. After being questioned by Reverend Hale, Tituba, Abigail, and Betty start accusing Goody Good, Goody Osburn, Sarah Good, Bridget Bishop, Goody Sibber, Alice Barrow, Goody Hawkins, Goody Bibber, and Goody Booth before the curtain falls. The women were surrounded by Hale and other officials in the town, who rejoiced as they named each witch. Anyone accused could be brought to trial as a result of just one accuser's testimony. We should notice that Bedlam's chorus of screaming accusations came from Tituba, Abigail, and Betty when they were being questioned about what they did in the forest, and accusing others was clearly a means by which they could distract from their being further questioned and investigated themselves. The chaos of this scene climaxed in the eruption of a chorus of “Hush Little Baby,” ending with all the characters on stage singing while looking directly at the audience. The choice of “Hush Little Baby” was especially powerful because it is a lullaby and seemed to signify how the general and random accusations of these women would lead to the “putting to rest” of investigations and of actual lives. The accusers are freed, but the accused are killed. —Lauren BonnerI found it fascinating how Bedlam presented the idea of voluntary sexual repression within Salem, an idea about which Arthur Miller was also very interested throughout his plays. In the climax of act 1, Betty and Abigail started shouting names of alleged witches. As the shouting grew, the other characters got more excited; Mrs. Putnam even spanked Mr. Putnam. While a seemingly unexpected and distasteful action, it made a lot of sense in the world of Salem that Bedlam offered the audience. The fact that the witchcraft accusations and these sexually suggestive actions occurred simultaneously articulated that the people of Salem had come to use accusing others of witchcraft as a way to satiate their suppressed sexual needs, while still believing they were following the Bible. Miller and Bedlam are raising the question, what happens when we as a society restrict our most basic animal instincts? Using this same lens, I found the flashlights the cast often used to be quite illuminating (literally). When Proctor and Abigail shone flashlights on each other, their shadows stood in front of the rings of light as if they were saints, drawing the contrast between holy and sinister, light and dark. title: Transnational Teacher Educators: Narratives on Multilingualism and Teaching
abstract: Continuing growth in immigration in the U.S. and other countries worldwide means an increased number of speakers of languages other than English or other national languages in classrooms, thus raising a need for teachers prepared for linguistically diverse student populations. While recent research in teaching and teacher education has pointed to different multilingual approaches, such as translanguaging and translingual practices, their implementation is influenced by monolingual and standard language ideologies and practices in classrooms. That is, schools and teachers demand standard English or standard versions of national languages in classrooms and restrict the use of other languages known by students. With myopic understandings of multilingualism, teacher education programs negate the experiences and possibilities of transnational teachers and teacher educators. In this dissertation, I explored the narratives of five transnational Indian/Indian American teacher educators about their language backgrounds, ideologies, and multilingual experiences. The dissertation answered the following research questions: 1. What are the language and literacy histories, ideologies, and teaching experiences of transnational Indian teacher educators (including doctoral students and tenured/tenure track/non-tenure track faculty)? 2. What kind of knowledge(s), practice(s), and lived experience(s) with multilingualism guide these transnational teacher educators to engage teacher candidates in exploring complex language issues in education in the U.S.? 3. What do stories of transnational teacher educators reveal about dynamic understandings of multilingualism that could inform the field of teacher education in the U.S.? I conducted interviews with five participants who identified as Indian/Indian American and worked as teacher educators in different areas of specialization in teacher education in the U.S. Jean Clandinin's approach to narrative inquiry informed the research design and the data analysis in the study. The participants narrated their multilingual experiences while growing up in India/U.S. The findings reveal the different ways in which teacher educators have interpreted and implemented their understanding of multilingualism in their areas of specialization in teacher education. The teacher educators also revealed the emotional entanglements with their experiences with the English language and its impact on multilingual learners. The implications from the study are of value to teacher educators, school leaders, and teachers working with linguistically diverse students in K-12 educational settings. title: Integrating Pine Forest High School, Fayetteville, North Carolina
abstract: Integrating Pine Forest High School, Fayetteville, North Carolina H. Louise Searles (bio) Click for larger view View full resolution For ten years, I attended public school with black Americans. But for a period during my last two years, I was the only black student at Pine Forest High, a historically white public school. H. Louise “Sparkle” Searles, courtesy of the author. [End Page 38] Most folks know August 28, 1963, as the March on Washington, but for me, it has another very profound meaning. It was the beginning of my every day walk with death for nine months—the start of Public School Integration in Fayetteville, North Carolina. For ten years, I attended public school with black Americans. But for a period during my last two years, I was the only black student at Pine Forest High, a historically white public school. Distracted by a fun-filled summer, I didn’t think much about my safety as the first day at my new school approached. But on the actual morning, just seven days shy of my sixteenth birthday, I was sure it was my last day on this earth. Terrified, I stood on Highway 210 with my sister Henrietta and our cousin, Robert King, waiting for bus 444 to pick us up. When it arrived, I stepped on first, followed by my sister and Robert, to find all of the seats taken. We thus stood for the 10-minute ride to the next stop, Spring Lake Elementary School, where Henrietta and Robert got off with other children. I found a seat. It was a lonely ride with a lot of mumbling, and I dreamt about my funeral until we stopped at the College Lakes subdivision. A young man got on and noticed the one empty seat by me, but instead of sitting down, he stood in the aisle until we reached the school. I remember saying to myself, “Stand up, you pimple-faced rascal. I did!” which made me laugh inside. When we arrived, there were no spectators. Still, my fear increased. Quickly, I made the decision to be the last to leave the bus. After everyone departed, I turned to the bus driver and said, “I will get off and walk with you into the building.” She didn’t respond but her look conveyed that she didn’t want to be seen with me. And further, that she didn’t want me riding her bus. She eyed me through the rearview mirror and parked the bus on the front row, then we left together. My knees stiffened on the walk across the parking lot. And when we entered the building, my stomach turned. I sensed hatred—a feeling that was very new to me and that I didn’t know how to process. A young man approached and whispered “traitor,” a comment directed at the bus driver, not me. Gasping, she touched her throat and replied, “I didn’t, she wanted …” I kept walking and didn’t see her again until it was time to board the bus. On the way to my homeroom, some students yelled angry, nasty words. I had been told not to address any outbursts or name-calling, so I kept walking, looking straight ahead as I did. Homerooms were off-limits until the first bell rang. Standing outside of the classroom, a female student approached me with her fist balled up. “How much is the naacp paying you to come here?” she asked. I didn’t answer—just looked straight into her eyes. Her hair was teased all over and very stiff. Her hair doesn’t move, I thought to myself. It doesn’t shake. She was wearing penny loafers with the penny in the little slot on top of her shoes, her skirt was a wrap-around that tied in the front, and the blouse was white with brown vertical pin stripes and a little round collar. I had not been introduced to such fashion before. [End Page 39] Finally, the bell rang and the door to homeroom opened. As I went into the classroom of Ms. Edna Jones, no one wanted to sit next to me. Not even the ones Ms. Jones...

title: Teaching, Improvising, Galumphing?
abstract: It is almost two years since I stopped teaching in a secondary school in Magandjin/Brisbane, Australia. I could feel myself cracking, becoming cynical and worn down by the expectations of the education system—a system that, I felt, was less and less interested in the people involved and more interested in standardisation and the data and results these people produced. I could feel my teaching becoming restricted by external values that ran counter to my own. My individuality and ethics as a person with experiences and thoughts were becoming less and less important. The ideas and wonderings of my students had diminishing space in which to be heard and considered. I felt I needed some time away. Teacher and scholar Margie Appel explains this well, highlighting a professional and systemic imbalance in Australian schools perniciously affecting teachers, noting a lack of professional autonomy, stifled creativity for teachers and students, and an absence of trust in teachers from school leaders. Black feminist educator and critic bell hooks reflects on her own experiences of needing time away from teaching. She describes a sense of gloom, her diminishing energy, and the sense her classroom was beginning to feel like “a closed-down space” (Teaching Community 13). She writes that she no longer had the energy to cope with the systemic and cultural “obstacles” that had always been there. She too keenly felt a need for some time away from teaching to reconsider and reflect, to create an opportunity for herself to “think of new ways to be immersed in teaching” (Teaching Community 21). hooks’s writing is honest and sounds deeply with me. There is sadness in her realisation­—a mourning for something lost and a recognition of something that cannot be unfelt. But there is also hope and possibility and strength as she continues to teach in a new and renewed way. These teacherly feelings draw me to communication scholar Bryant Keith Alexander’s reflexive concept of standing in the wake. Alexander uses the metaphor of standing in the wake to “represent a time after experience for critical reflection” (98), describing this phrase as “a metaphor for reflexivity, a critical act of standing in the present critically reflecting on past experience, a positionality” (105). He describes the wake as “the rack left in water by a vessel or any other body moving through it” (103) and “a stream of turbulence” (104). In my case, time away from high school teaching has afforded me distance from it and a new perspective on what my teaching might be/be becoming. While this decision has, in some ways, created turbulence, it has also provided a stillness and calm from the pressures and fast tempos of a high school. I am standing in the wake of my teaching and teacherlyness but still very much in, and surrounded by, the waters of it. To clarify, this article is not me reflecting on my teaching experience—the number of years spent doing so, the subjects, the specific lessons, the year levels, and so on—but rather an account of my experience teaching. How do I experience teaching? How does my teaching feel? Curriculum scholar Ted Aoki encourages us to shift our educational discourse away from technical rationality and the doing of teaching and towards the presence and thoughtfulness found in the being of teaching. He reminds us that in our attempts to understand teaching we should try to “reorient ourselves … so that we can see and hear our doings as teaching harboured within pedagogical being, so we can see and hear who we are as teachers” (197, emphasis in original). Aoki’s writings resonate with musical terminology and sonorous observations. He suggests the improvisation of curriculum, the sound and the silence found in classrooms. He asks us to listen to, to hear, to be attuned to our teaching, to move beyond the “ocularcentrism in Western epistemology” (xvi). He is feeling teaching. When I think of my experience teaching, it is these ideas of sounds, attunement, feeling, and presence that call out to me. In what follows, I stand in the wake, reflecting upon my teaching and my teacherlyness, focussing on the feelings of improvising, joy, and galumphing. Teaching feels like improvising but not in a metaphorical sense. I am an improvising musician, taught and playing mostly in the jazz tradition, and the doing and the being of teaching feels remarkably similar to the doing and being of playing this music. Improvisation isn’t unprepared, but it can be unpredictable. Improvisation can be interactive, responsive, and highly collaborative. Artistic freedom and expression can be found within structures and rules. Exemplary in this area are written works by Keith Sawyer, Ingrid Monson, Daniel Fischlin, and musical works: Spirograph Studies, and Ron Miles. Recently, I’ve begun rehearsing again with a jazz trio: saxophone, double bass, and drums. I play the drums. We are playing original music written by the saxophone player, Luke, for a series of performances and an upcoming recording, but also just to play music together. We’ve been playing together on and off for several years, but from the first rehearsal, this time around felt different. Luke writes what he fondly refers to as sketches of songs: ideas that grab him unexpectedly and demand to be written down immediately. He’s been notating these ideas differently, in a digital notebook (as opposed to musical notation software), as there is a freedom in the process of writing this way, he says, where the unfinished idea that tumbles out feels less fixed and aesthetically more open to being developed, changed, questioned (for example, see fig. 1). As a fellow ensemble member, my experience of this music is also different: the very fact that the notes don’t look as final on the page as notation software renders, there is ambiguity as to placement, and mistakes where Luke has written something 'wrong', or forgotten to include something harmonically or rhythmically important, means there is possibility and openness in this music. The sketches are inviting us all in to learn them and wanting our ideas and voices to join them. Fig. 1: Eerie/Beautiful. Image courtesy of Luke. This music visually welcomes collaboration and questions. This is music unsure what it might sound like. And we are musicians wondering how we might play it and how we might make it sound. Alongside these sketches, Luke tells us his inspiration or intentions for each song. These can be very clear or quite vague. But regardless, there is something within each sketch that resonates strongly within him that he wants to share, even if it is just the joyful feeling of playing the melody. The experience of playing this music and playing in this ensemble is how I try to teach in the classroom. What I mean by this is that there is openness, opportunity, and unexpectedness in these rehearsals but there is also preparation, a perspective, and a possible outcome. We three meet knowing that we will be learning and making music together but not knowing what that might sound like or how far we might get in that process. Education theorist Gert Biesta writes about what he believes to be two fundamental elements of teaching: showing and explaining (44–8). The teacher shows something they think is interesting, or worth noticing, to their students, and offers them an explanation of what they feel is noteworthy, but also gives their students space to critique it, consider it in their own way, and offer their thoughts. Critical education theorist Paulo Freire provides a similar notion that he terms “a little introductory exposition” (123), in which a teacher makes a brief presentation of a subject and then students and teacher analyse and question together the subject and presentation. He writes that in this way, “the teacher challenges the students, who thereupon question themselves and question the teacher, and thereby share in plumbing the depths of, developing, the initial exposition” (123). In this process, the teacherly act becomes less about instruction and more about invitation. Students are invited into the teacher’s thinking but do not conform to it, nor are they limited by it. The object and subject provide an opportunity for individual and collaborative thinking and reflection on the object and the self as the students bring their selves to bear on the object. I feel this is what Luke is offering to us in these rehearsals. Just as students and teacher in the classroom environments I foster, we three too gather around the thing Luke is showing us and explaining to us (his composition) and bring our perspectives to bear on it. We all regard it, think about it, play and improvise with it, and with each other and through this process we come to know this composition, ourselves, and each other a little more. We each bring different perspectives to bear on this composition and, as such, may notice different things or derive meanings different from Luke’s, which are then shared with the group sonically through our music-making and through discussions during and after each rehearsal. These rehearsals are full of risk-taking, mistakes, conversation, listening, joy: improvisation. These rehearsals are full of the sound of learning and teaching and creating. These rehearsals are lessons. Our music-making, our improvising, is our learning. This feels like my teaching. Teaching feels joyful; teaching is joyful. title: Notes on Contributing Authors
abstract: Mellonee Burnim gave the 2021 Charles Seeger Lecture at the Society for Ethnomusicology Annual Meeting. She is professor emerita in the Department of Folklore and Ethnomusicology and retired Director of the Archives of African American Music and Culture at Indiana University-Bloomington. At IU, she served as Director of the Ethnomusicology Institute and chairperson in the Department of African American and African Diaspora Studies. She holds a BME (cum laude) in music education from North Texas State University (1971), a MM in ethnomusicology from the University of Wisconsin-Madison (1976), and a PhD in ethnomusicology from Indiana University (1980). As an ethnomusicologist with a specialization in African American religious music, Burnim has done fieldwork and led choral music workshops on African American religious music across the United States, as well as in Cuba and Malawi. She is co-editor, with Portia Maultsby, of African American Music: An Introduction (Routledge 2006), now in its second edition (2015).Corinna Campbell (M.M. Bowling Green State University, Ph.D. Harvard University) is Associate Professor of Music at Williams College. Her scholarship on popular culture and folkloric performance among the Suriname Maroons includes her first manuscript, The Cultural Work: Maroon Performance in Paramaribo, Suriname (Wesleyan University Press 2020) and the book chapter, “Modeling Cultural Adaptability: Maroon Cosmopolitanism and the Banamba Contest,” in Maroon Cosmopolitics: Personhood, Creativity, and Incorporation, edited by Olivia Maria Gomes da Cunha (Brill 2018), winner of the 2019 Joann Kealiinohomoku Award. Her research has been funded by the Fulbright Institute, the David Rockefeller Center for Latin American Studies, and the Oakley Center for the Humanities.Timothy P.A. Cooper is an anthropologist and ethnographic filmmaker studying religion, ethics, and media in contemporary Pakistan. Currently a Leverhulme Trust / Isaac Newton Trust Early Career Research Fellow in the Department of Social Anthropology at the University of Cambridge, he is affiliated with the Max-Planck-Cambridge Centre for Ethics, Economy, and Social Change and is a College Research Associate at King's College, Cambridge. His work has appeared in the Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute, Comparative Studies in Society and History, Material Religion, and the Journal of Material Culture. His first book, Public Demand: Film, Islam, and Atmosphere in a Pakistani Marketplace, is under contract with Columbia University Press. The manuscript was awarded the 2022 Claremont Prize in the Study of Religion.Joseph Maurer is a Lecturer in Music at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. He researches music education in Chicago immigrant communities, maritime music revivalism, and online aesthetic formations. His public and nonprofit-sector work includes research, strategic planning, curriculum design, and program evaluation for Chicago arts education organizations and public schools. Prior to his doctoral studies, Joe worked with high school students as a college access counselor in Providence, RI and Boston, MA.David W. Samuels-MacKinnon is Associate Professor in the Music Department at New York University. He is the author of Putting a Song On Top Of It: Expression and Identity on the San Carlos Apache Reservation (University of Arizona Press 2004). He has published extensively on the intersections of music, language, poetics, popular culture, and vernacular modernities.Bell Yung, an ethnomusicologist specializing on China, is Emeritus Professor at the University of Pittsburgh, where he retired in 2012, and Affiliate Professor at the University of Washington. He has also taught at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong University, University of California at Davis, and Cornell University, and is a recipient of research grants from Guggenheim, Ford, Mellon, National Endowment of the Humanities, Fulbright, and others. He has published twelve books and over 100 articles in journals and in edited volumes, in English and in Chinese. His most recent publications are “The Scholar and the Courtesan: Songs on the Pearl River's Flower Boats” (2022), “Wu Song Kills the Tiger: Transcription and Translation of a Cantonese Narrative Song from a Live Performance, with an Introduction” (2021), “From Humble Beginnings to Qin Master: the Remarkable Cross-Fertilization of Folk and Elite Cultures in Yao Bingyan's Dapu Music” (2021), and the Chinese language edition of his 2008 book The Last of China's Literati: The Music, Poetry and Life of Tsar Teh-yun (2022). Bell Yung was born in Shanghai, grew up in Hong Kong, and received higher education in the U.S. with degrees of Engineering Physics (B.Sc., University of California, Berkeley), Physics (Ph.D., Massachusetts Institute of Technology), and Music (Ph.D., Harvard University). In 2012 he was awarded an Honorary Doctorate from the Chinese University of Hong Kong. Website: bellyung.weebly.com

title: A new scientific journal takes the scene: The birth of reviews of modern physics
abstract: Review articles are indispensable elements of the modern physics literature. The number of journals devoted to reviews has been steadily growing, and some of these journals are highly valued by the physics community. Physicists are eager to publish in journals such as Annual Reviews (1932–present), Reports on Progress in Physics (1934–present) and, most of all, Reviews of Modern Physics (RMP) (1929–present). With its impressive Journal Citation Reports' Five-Year Impact Factor of 51.882 reached in 2012, the RMP stands out as one of the most prestigious physics journals according to current criteria for the allocation of authority. Already in the 1930s, some of the papers published in RMP played pivotal roles in furthering research in newly-emerging fields of physics by summarizing the latest achievements and by indicating promising future lines of investigation. Recall, e.g., the review on relativistic cosmology published in 1931 by the US mathematical physicist Howard P. Robertson 1, Enrico Fermi's paper on quantum electrodynamics of 1932 2, and the three review articles on nuclear physics that Hans A. Bethe and co-workers published in 1936–37 frequently referred to as "Bethe's Bible" 3-5. One of the main reasons underlying the success of this journal was that, in the 1930s, the USA had come to rival Germany as the leading country in physics research as a consequence of dramatic political and economical transformations. A by-product of this shift was that English gradually became the leading language in the physics literature. In this shifting context, the RMP occupied a niche that was still open because, when the first number appeared in July 1929, it was the only academic periodic journal that published exclusively scholarly review articles in physics. Various forms of review articles had long appeared in the German-language physics literature. The section "Zusammenfassende Bearbeitungen" in Physikalische Zeitschrift (1899–1945), papers appearing in Die Naturwissenschaften (1913–present), and, especially, the large reviews on specific subjects collected in the Encyklopädie [Enzyklopädie] der Mathematischen Wissenschaften (1898–1935) as well as in the series of books entitled Handbuch der Physik (1926–1933), were well-established ways through which German-language physicists dealt with the need for review articles. Although in a more unsystematic manner, review articles in physics had already appeared in non-German-language journals, including English-language mainstream publications, such as Nature (1869–present), Science (1880–present), and the Journal of the Franklin Institute (1826–present). Nevertheless, insofar as the format of the scientific periodical is concerned, RMP probably was the first journal of its kind.1 The process leading to the establishment of RMP was quite controversial. The novelty of this type of journal entailed a series of questions, anxieties and concerns that were clearly exposed by the physicists who corresponded with the proponent of this endeavor: the professor of physics of the University of Minnesota John Torrence Tate, Sr., who had become the editor of Physical Review (1893–present) in 1926 (see Fig. 1). Since the early days of his editorial venture, Tate pursued the well-defined target of increasing the journal's international prestige 7. Tate tried to do so by improving the refereeing process rather than by modifying the policy for contributing authors of Physical Review. There, one could only publish articles "devoted to actual new results" and with only an extremely brief, if any, summary of previous work.2 In October 1928, Tate proposed a deep modification in the editorial activities of the American Physical Society (APS). He sent an unusual letter to 53 APS members, chosen among the most authoritative experts in different branches of theoretical, experimental, applied, and industrial physics. It prompted the idea of publishing a "new type of journal in Physics—a journal in which would appear reports and critical comments on the various branches of current thoughts and research." According to Tate, his fellow physicists were implicitly recognizing the need for synthetic reports in various ways, such as in the symposia held at APS meetings as well as in the seminars organized in universities and research laboratories. The target of the proposed journal was to extend such kinds of discussions to a wider audience through articles similar to those published in the "Zusammenfassende Bearbeitungen" section of Physikalische Zeitschrift. In the US physics literature nothing similar existed, Tate argued, apart from the up-to-date summaries of entire domains of research in the Bulletins of the National Research Council (1919–1950), which were written by selected commissions of experts. He maintained that it was necessary to produce a different kind of literature "a little less formal and formidable to prepare than these Bulletins." Tate concluded his letter asking for general comments on his proposal before he would present the idea at the Council of the APS 9. In spite of his strong personal commitment to this idea, Tate's letter was void of details as for the actual format that both the articles and the journal should assume. Some fundamental features remained unclear, which some replies explicitly complained about. This vagueness in the definition of the new journal's structure resulted in Tate's respondents expressing divergent ideas concerning the exact shape and scope of the future journal. Among the questions addressed by the 48 physicists who replied, the most consequential one probably was: Which articles or journals in the existing scientific literature represented the best example to follow?3 This fundamental issue implied other questions raised by Tate's correspondents: Why are review articles necessary in the USA? Whom is the journal directed to? Who should write the articles? What should the distinction be between this journal and other similar scientific publications? How often should it appear? What should be its relationship to the Physical Review? The way in which the replies addressed these questions shows that there was no universal agreement either on the role the journal should play within the US physics community, or on the strategy the editors should pursue. In addition, although many recognized the value of publishing review articles, some—including the highly influential experimentalist Robert A. Millikan—strongly disagreed with Tate's plan 11. One of the most interesting features in this hodgepodge of responses concerns the opposing views on the relationship between Tate's proposal and the rapid expansion in the number of physicists, specializations, and, consequently, journals. Some physicists lamented that a new publication was undesirable because it was impossible to subscribe to—and read—so many scientific journals. Yet, others noted that a journal dedicated to reviews could be very useful in order to keep in touch with recent advances in the various areas of physics. What the latter physicists were seeking was a "pre-digested summary of a new field" in which they "have begun to acquire an interest" 12. Digestion was a recurring metaphor in the expressions physicists employed to express their belief that review articles were a necessity. The impressive number of publications, the growth in the number of fields, the excessive specialization, all were jeopardizing the physicists' wish to maintain an up-to-date knowledge of the most relevant advances in what they considered a unified scientific discipline: physics. The different views on how the physics community should face the ongoing information explosion were related to very different ideas about the audience the journal should aim for.4 In his letter to the APS members, Tate implicitly held that the novel periodical was intended primarily for US professional physicists: By means of review articles, experts from different fields could share their knowledge with specialists in other fields. Still more implicitly, the journal could be a way to keep the physics community unified by challenging the perils of an uncontrolled compartmentalization. The theoretical physicist Edward U. Condon provided an in-depth analysis of how this could be accomplished. Condon believed the growth of sectoral specializations to be a dangerous tendency in the US physics community, and here the scientific literature was of no help. His enthusiasm toward Tate's proposal was motivated by the belief that the new kind of journal was essential for US physicists to increase their prestige, especially in theoretical physics 15. The view that professional physicists should be the main—and perhaps the only—audience of the new journal was not widely shared, however. Most correspondents believed that this type of scientific literature would attract various categories of readers: college students, college and high school teachers, laymen with scientific interests, and industrial researchers. Those who proposed to consider a larger audience saw the journal as a means for the APS to "extend greatly its membership and its sphere of influence" 16. Furthermore, Tate's correspondents raised concerns about the profile of the possible authors of the critical reviews. Many complained that to find adequate authors would be difficult. The main obstacle was that, on the one hand, the author should be an authoritative expert of the specific field he was writing on; on the other hand, it was important that brilliant physicists did not invest too much time away from doing original research in writing such articles. The profile question was also related to what most correspondents believed to be a real obstacle. As the head of the Physics Department at Cornell, the experimentalist Ernest G. Merritt, clearly expressed, the writing of review papers was time-consuming and there was serious doubt "whether the [author] benefits any where near in proportion to the effort and time involved" 17. The same issue was elaborated on by the industrial physicist Karl K. Darrow who, on the contrary, considered this kind of literature fundamental. He had made the writing of review articles his main activity since 1923, when he began disseminating recent advances in physics within the Bell Telephone Laboratories through his reports published in the Bell System Technical Journal (1922–1983).5 Darrow suspected that "many have the notion that [review articles] are not 'original', whatever that may mean; and that a review, synopsis or Bericht, no matter how good, is inferior to any not-previously-performed experiment or calculation, no matter how trivial." As a consequence, Darrow concluded, many believed that "the preparation of such an article brings no reward in appreciation" 19. Put succinctly, at the time Tate proposed RMP, review articles were still considered as second-rank publications. Among the 48 physicists who answered Tate's letter, only 13 were willing to write a review paper in the near future. The others were either doubtful or decisively negative, the main reason being that they had no time to spare. Given these difficulties, it was proposed that the authors of the review articles should be physicists whose talent was to summarize and disseminate original research made by others. In particular, four physicists mentioned Darrow's papers in the Bell System Technical Journal as exemplars. The underlying idea was that a few physicists not directly involved in original research could specialize in producing this kind of literature. As for the question whether such a journal was necessary or not, many correspondents shared Tate's conviction that critical review articles were important—albeit for different reasons and from different perspectives—but objected to the need for a new journal entirely dedicated to such papers. Some asked for a modification in the editorial policy of Science to make it the main organ for publishing up-to-date physics reports. Others maintained that Nature was already publishing such material. Still others held that the German-language physicists were already accomplishing this task successfully, and perhaps one could just translate what was being published elsewhere. For those who recognized the need for review papers in physics, the main reason for objecting to the launching of a new journal was financial. The main target of the APS should remain the publication of Physical Review and a new publication should not distract attention from this primary endeavor. After having received all the responses, Tate prepared a resumé, which he presented before the APS Council in December 1928. While Tate briefly summarized the different positions, in the resumé he somewhat overstated the positive reactions by amplifying the number of replies who agreed on the need for taking care of a new publication. Tate emphasized that almost all the respondents agreed that the review articles were "necessary," at the same time playing down the number of opposing views and the reasons underlying their negative—or doubtful—reaction. Four months later, the first announcement of the new journal appeared in the pages of Physical Review 20. Many of the suggestions made by Tate's correspondents, especially concerning the audience, were fully integrated in the official statement appearing in the first issues of the quarterly RMP, which was temporarily called Physical Review Supplement in 1929.6 In order to explain to potential subscribers why they should spend about $4 per year (corresponding approximately to $54.50 in 2013 according to the U.S. Consumer Price Index inflation calculator) for an additional physics journal, the editors were very explicit on the rationale underlying their decision to launch the new publication: "Its purpose is to provide those interested in the developments in physics with comprehensive, authoritative, and timely discussions of the problems which are, at the present time, of special interest and importance. It is intended that in so far as possible these discussions shall be written in such form as to interest and to inform those who are not specialists in the subjects under discussion. It is hoped that the studies appearing in [it] will give to the specialist the benefit of the view point, in a broad sense, of other specialists; to the student, a background of critical knowledge and an adequate bibliography of source material; to those whose time is absorbed in the teaching of physics, a stimulating account of the forward movement of their science" 22. The general picture that emerges by looking at the rapid and dynamical process that took place from Tate's proposal in October 1928 to the publication of the first issue of the new journal in July 1929 is that the final shape of RMP was the result of a negotiation between very different conceptions of the journal. They in turn depended on different needs felt by the US physicists involved, different opinions about the virtues and the deficiencies of the US physics community, and even different views on the role of review articles. It was a collective endeavour in which partial images of the journal were implemented and enriched by other visions, sometimes radically different. It is evident that the main driving idea leading to the construction of RMP was Tate's belief that a journal dedicated to review articles of physics would be seminal. It is likewise clear that Tate did not have a very precise idea on how to create such a journal and was very receptive to the various contrasting impulses coming from fellow physicists as for the final shape of the journal. The discussion that Tate started and that anticipated the birth of RMP went well beyond its original limited scope. This discussion became a preferred way for the US community of physicists to reflect on itself and on its rapidly changing needs. The archival research was supported by a grant-in-aid of the Friends of the Center for History of Physics, American Institute of Physics. I am deeply indebted to Christian Joas, Dieter Hoffman and Skúli Sigurdsson for discussions and comments on a previous version of the paper.
